questions.question: Pseudo-classes vs pseudo-elements — what's the difference, and which ones solve real UI problems?
questions.title: Pseudo Map
questions.direct_answer: PSEUDO-CLASSES select ELEMENTS in a STATE (no new box): :hover, :focus-visible (the accessible focus — only shows for keyboard, not every click), :disabled, :checked (CSS-only toggles via the checkbox/radio hack), :nth-child() / :nth-of-type() (structural — 'every 3rd row'), :not() / :is() / :where() (selector combinators — the modern specificity trio), :has() ('parent selector' — .card:has(img) styles a card THAT CONTAINS an image — the 2023 unlock that ended the decades-long gap), :empty, :placeholder-shown (float-label pattern). PSEUDO-ELEMENTS create/generated TARGETS (::before/::after content boxes, ::placeholder, ::selection, ::first-line, ::marker for list bullets) — they need the content property and double-colon syntax. The classic patterns: decorative icons/labels (::before with content), clear-field buttons via :placeholder-shown + :not(:focus), grid stripe with nth-child(even), and :has() for form validation states (input:invalid + a wrapper :has(:invalid) message).

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The map with the working patterns, verified:

```css
/* STATE selection — pseudo-classes */
input:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--brand); }  /* keyboard focus
                                                            ONLY — clicks stay
                                                            clean but keyboard
                                                            users SEE it */
input:not(:focus):not(:placeholder-shown) + label { top: -8px; } /* float label:
   label floats ONLY when field has content and is unfocused */

/* STRUCTURAL — striping and slicing */
tr:nth-child(even) { background: var(--surface); }        /* zebra tables */
li:nth-of-type(3n) { border-inline-end: none; }           /* grid edge cleanup */

/* THE PARENT SELECTOR — :has() */
.card:has(img) { padding-top: 0; }              /* card WITH an image differs */
form:has(input:user-invalid) .submit { opacity: .6; }   /* disable submit when a
                                                          field is invalid */

/* GENERATED BOXES — pseudo-elements (content: required) */
.required::after { content: ' *'; color: red; }   /* the accessible asterisk */
a[href^='http']::after { content: ' ↗'; }        /* external-link marker */
::selection { background: var(--brand); }        /* global selection color */
li::marker { color: var(--brand); }              /* list bullet styling */
```

The distinction (the one-line rule): a pseudo-CLASS answers 'is this element in state X' (hover, focus, checked, 3rd child, has-invalid-input) — it selects EXISTING elements; a pseudo-ELEMENT creates a VIRTUAL box you can style (::before/::after content, ::placeholder, ::first-line) — you can't put that box in the HTML because it isn't an element until CSS generates it. The single-colon legacy (:before) still parses; the double-colon form is the modern distinction marker.

The a11y-critical detail (the focus story): :focus applies on EVERY focus (mouse clicks too — the 'why is there a ring on click' complaint); :focus-visible shows the ring only where the browser infers KEYBOARD input — the accessible default everyone should switch to. The companion: :focus-within styles a parent whose DESCENDANT is focused (the input-group highlight pattern) — a different selector than :focus.

The checkbox-hack context (stateful CSS without JS) and its limits: :checked + sibling selectors drive pure-CSS tabs/toggles — but they break history integration, a11y roles, and scale poorly — the reason JS drives real components while :checked stays for small visual states. :has() is the modern replacement for most of those hacks (style the PARENT by child state directly), with graceful degradation: wrap :has() rules so older browsers keep the base layout.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    PC[pseudo-CLASS: element in a state] --> ST[hover focus-visible checked nth-child]
    PC --> HAS[:has — select the parent by its contents]
    PE[pseudo-ELEMENT: generated virtual box] --> GEN[::before ::after ::marker ::selection ::placeholder]
    FV[:focus-visible] --> A11Y[ring for keyboard, clean for mouse]
    FW[:focus-within] --> PARENT2[style the parent while a child is focused]
    CON[content property] --> REQ[required for ::before / ::after to render]
    CB[checkbox + :checked hacks] --> LIMIT[no history no a11y scale — :has replaces most]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The selector-level-4 combinators (the trio that changed selector architecture): :not() in Level 3 took a SIMPLE selector; Level 4 takes a COMPLEX selector list (:not(.a .b)) — and :is()/:where() take lists too, with the specificity asymmetry (:is takes the max of its arguments, :where zeroes them). The practical consequence: :is(header, main) .content {} replaces repetition with ONE rule, and :where() wrapping third-party resets means user rules override with any specificity — the modern stylesheet-management pattern.

The generated-content mechanics (what ::before/after really are): pseudo-elements are CSS-generated CHILD boxes (first/last child of the originating element) — they inherit, they can be absolutely positioned, and content can be a string, an attr() reference (content: attr(data-label) — the tooltip/copy pattern with zero extra markup), a url() image, or a counter() (the numbered-list numbering machinery: counter-increment + counters() for NESTED numbering — the '1.2.3' outlines, glossaries, and legal docs numbering built in pure CSS). Pseudo-elements are NOT in the DOM: no event listeners, no text selection on some engines, invisible to most assistive tech — decorative content ONLY, never information.

The :has() family in depth (the relational unlock): :has() accepts the full selector grammar — :has(> img), :has(+ .ad) (the NEXT-SIBLING relationship — 'a headline followed by an ad'), and composes with everything (.card:has(.title:hover)). The implementation story worth one line: browsers resisted it for two decades over performance (invalidation across the whole tree on any DOM change); the modern invalidation-set approach made it shippable (Chrome 105+ / Safari 15.4+ / Firefox 121+) — and today it replaces a whole class of wrapper-divs-for-styling and checkbox hacks, while JS feature-detection (CSS.supports('selector(:has(*))')) gates the progressive enhancement.
